Clickstream analytics

Every tap and page view on a busy site sends a tiny event to you. Hundreds of millions pile up each day. Analysts open dashboards to ask what happened this hour. Never drop an event, and keep the storage bill under control as the pile grows. Practise this medium system design problem for free, with no sign-up.

Play this problem

The brief

Every tap and page view on a busy site sends a tiny event to you. Hundreds of millions pile up each day. Analysts open dashboards to ask what happened this hour. Never drop an event, and keep the storage bill under control as the pile grows.

Think of the page-view tracking behind a product analytics tool.

Users, scale and requirements

Who uses it
Events from 30 million visitors a month (approx.)
Audience in plain numbers
30,000,000 people per month
Normal peak
≈ 8,000 requests per second
Request mix
Analytics event: 99%; Report: 1%
Speed for 99 of 100 requests
Report: ≈ 30,000 ms
Successful requests
99.9%
Data safety
No acknowledged write may be lost.
Monthly budget
≈ $72,000
Data at rest
≈ 20 TB
Where users are
North America: 50%; Europe: 30%; Asia Pacific: 20%
Home region
North America
Waiting deadlines
Analytics event: 3,600 seconds; Report: 3,600 seconds

≈ marks an approximation, just as in the game. Waiting deadlines measure the age of queued work and are separate from interactive response time.

  • About 300 million events a day, each about 0.5 KB (approx.).
  • Roughly 150 GB of new raw data a day (approx.).
  • All numbers are rough approximations.

Questions that shape the design

Must a dashboard be real-time?

A few minutes behind is fine. Nobody needs the exact second.

Can an event be counted twice?

Rarely and a little is acceptable for page views, but lost events are not.

How long do we keep raw events?

Recent data stays handy for a month. Older data is rarely read and can go to cheap storage.

The traffic day

Consumer traffic, busiest in the evening. The clock covers 00:00 to 24:00 in the home region. Events add pressure on top of that normal traffic.

  1. 20:00 · Viral spike

    A post blows up. Traffic climbs to several times normal within minutes.

    Traffic reaches 2 times the scheduled load; rises over 600 seconds, holds for 3,600 seconds and eases over 3,600 seconds.

  2. 14:00 · Metrics explosion

    Someone adds a user id to a metric label. Series count jumps 20 times and so does the bill.

    Duration: ≈ 21,600 seconds.

  3. 16:00 · Cost blowout

    A crawler hits uncached pages all day, and every pay-per-use part of the bill multiplies.

    Traffic reaches 1.5 times the scheduled load; rises over 600 seconds, holds for 21,600 seconds and eases over 600 seconds. Duration: ≈ 21,600 seconds.

What a strong design has to handle

  • Events arrive far faster than people read dashboards. What can sit between the two?
  • Acknowledge durable events and aggregate retries and late arrivals correctly.
  • Dashboards a few minutes behind are far cheaper than live ones, because summaries are built in batches.
  • Keeping raw events lets analysts ask new questions later, but storage grows every day. Tiering keeps it affordable.

Make a prediction, run a full traffic day, then compare the result. The in-game editorial opens after a finished day and includes measured reference designs.

Concepts to practise

  • Waiting instead of breaking
  • Hot, warm, cold and archive
